method_card.title: Newton's Laws, Momentum and Waves
steps: Pick the equation the question points to: \(F = ma\), \(p = mv\), \(v = f\lambda\) or \(T = 1/f\).
Convert to base units first: grams to kilograms, kHz to Hz, cm to metres.
For \(F = ma\) use the resultant force (driving force minus friction or weight).
Substitute, calculate, state the unit; use standard form for very large or small numbers.
method_card.content:
Newton's second law \(F = ma\) always uses the resultant force. If friction or weight acts, subtract it from the driving force first. Constant velocity means the resultant force is zero.

Momentum \(p = mv\) is conserved in collisions: total before equals total after. It is higher tier only.

Waves: \(v = f\lambda\), and period \(T = 1/f\). Convert frequency to hertz and lengths to metres before substituting. Check whether your board gives you the period equation.

exam_context.frequency: Very high. Force and wave calculations appear almost every year. Momentum is higher tier only but frequently tested.

bronze.display: A resultant force of 240 N acts on an 80 kg trolley. Calculate its acceleration.
bronze.hint: Rearrange F = ma to a = F ÷ m, then divide.

misconceptions.message: a = F ÷ m = 240 ÷ 80 = 3 m/s². Multiplying (240 × 80) is the slip.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(F = ma\). We want the acceleration, so rearrange to \(a = F \div m\).
guided_steps.hint: Read it straight from the question.
It is already in kg, no conversion needed.

guided_steps.say: Now divide.

guided_steps.done: It gives back 240 N, so a = 3 m/s².

bronze.display: Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 1500 kg car at 2 m/s².
bronze.hint: F = ma. Multiply mass by acceleration.

misconceptions.message: F = ma = 1500 × 2 = 3000 N. Dividing (1500 ÷ 2 = 750) is the slip; here you multiply.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(F = ma\). Force is the subject already, so no rearranging.
Multiply.

guided_steps.hint: Divide your force by the mass.
guided_steps.done: Back to 2 m/s², so F = 3000 N.

bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. Calculate its speed.
bronze.hint: v = f × λ. Multiply frequency by wavelength.

misconceptions.message: v = f × λ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m/s. Dividing (500 ÷ 0.68) gives about 735, but here you multiply.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\): speed equals frequency times wavelength.
Multiply.

guided_steps.hint: Divide your speed by the wavelength.
guided_steps.done: Back to 500 Hz, so v = 340 m/s.

bronze.display: A water wave has a speed of 2 m/s and a wavelength of 0.5 m. Calculate its frequency.
bronze.hint: Rearrange v = fλ to f = v ÷ λ.

misconceptions.message: f = v ÷ λ = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 Hz. Multiplying (2 × 0.5 = 1) is the slip.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\). We want frequency, so rearrange to \(f = v \div \lambda\).
Divide.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply your frequency by the wavelength.
guided_steps.done: Back to 2 m/s, so f = 4 Hz.

bronze.display: A 10 N force accelerates a 2 kg object. Calculate the acceleration.
bronze.hint: a = F ÷ m. Divide force by mass.

misconceptions.message: a = F ÷ m = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m/s². Multiplying (10 × 2 = 20) is the slip.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(F = ma\). We want acceleration, so \(a = F \div m\).
Divide.

guided_steps.done: Back to 10 N, so a = 5 m/s².

bronze.display: A wave has a frequency of 200 Hz. Calculate its period.

misconceptions.message: T = 1 ÷ f = 1 ÷ 200 = 0.005 s. Period and frequency are reciprocals; the answer is not 200.

guided_steps.say: Period and frequency are reciprocals: \(T = 1 \div f\).
Divide 1 by the frequency.
guided_steps.hint: 1 shared into 200 equal parts is a small decimal.

guided_steps.done: Back to 200 Hz, so T = 0.005 s.

bronze.display: Which equation links force, mass and acceleration?
bronze.hint: Newton's second law relates force, mass and acceleration.

misconceptions.message: Newton's second law: F = ma. p = mv is momentum, v = fλ is wave speed, W = mg is weight.

bronze.display: A wave has a speed of 330 m/s and a frequency of 660 Hz. Calculate the wavelength.
bronze.hint: Rearrange v = fλ to λ = v ÷ f.

misconceptions.message: λ = v ÷ f = 330 ÷ 660 = 0.5 m. Dividing the wrong way (660 ÷ 330 = 2) is the slip.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\). We want wavelength, so \(\lambda = v \div f\).
Divide.

guided_steps.done: Back to 330 m/s, so λ = 0.5 m.

silver.display: A car has a driving force of 3500 N and a friction force of 500 N. Its mass is 1200 kg. Calculate its acceleration.
silver.hint: Find the resultant force (driving minus friction) first, then a = F ÷ m.

misconceptions.message: Use the resultant force, not the driving force. Resultant = 3500 − 500 = 3000 N, so a = 3000 ÷ 1200 = 2.5 m/s². Using 3500 N gives about 2.92.
Divide the resultant by the mass: a = 3000 ÷ 1200 = 2.5 m/s², not 1200 ÷ 3000.

guided_steps.say: First find the resultant force: driving force minus friction.
guided_steps.hint: Take the friction off the driving force.

guided_steps.say: Now \(a = F \div m\) with the resultant force.

guided_steps.done: Back to 3000 N, so a = 2.5 m/s².

silver.display: A sound wave has a frequency of 2 kHz and a wavelength of 17 cm. Calculate the speed of sound.
silver.hint: Convert to Hz and metres first, then v = f × λ.

misconceptions.message: Convert 17 cm to 0.17 m first. v = 2000 × 0.17 = 340 m/s. Leaving it as 17 gives 34000.

guided_steps.say: Convert to base units first. \(v = f\lambda\) needs hertz and metres.
Now multiply.

guided_steps.hint: Divide your speed by the wavelength.
guided_steps.done: Back to 2000 Hz, so v = 340 m/s.

silver.display: A 500 g toy car is pushed with a force of 4 N. Friction is 2 N. Calculate its acceleration.
silver.hint: Convert grams to kg, subtract friction for the resultant, then a = F ÷ m.

misconceptions.message: Convert 500 g to 0.5 kg. Resultant = 4 − 2 = 2 N, so a = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 m/s². Using 500 kg gives 0.004.
Subtract friction first: resultant = 4 − 2 = 2 N, then a = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 m/s². Using 4 N gives 8.

guided_steps.say: Convert the mass, then find the resultant force.

guided_steps.hint: Take the friction off the push.

guided_steps.say: Now \(a = F \div m\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 2 N, so a = 4 m/s².

silver.display: A moving object of mass 4 kg has a momentum of 20 kg m/s. Calculate its velocity.
silver.hint: Rearrange p = mv to v = p ÷ m.

misconceptions.message: v = p ÷ m = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s. Multiplying (20 × 4 = 80) is the slip.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(p = mv\). We want velocity, so \(v = p \div m\).
Divide.

guided_steps.done: Back to 20 kg m/s, so v = 5 m/s.

silver.display: A microwave has a frequency of 2.45 GHz. The speed of EM waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the wavelength. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
silver.hint: Convert GHz to Hz (× 10⁹), then λ = v ÷ f.

misconceptions.message: 2.45 GHz = 2.45 × 10⁹ Hz. λ = v ÷ f = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ (2.45 × 10⁹) = 0.12 m. Dividing the other way gives about 8.2.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\). We want wavelength, so \(\lambda = v \div f\). First convert GHz.
guided_steps.pre: 2.45 GHz written as 2.45 × 10ⁿ hertz: the power n =
guided_steps.hint: Giga means times a thousand million, 10⁹.

guided_steps.say: Now the powers of ten.

guided_steps.hint: Move the decimal one place left. To 2 d.p.

guided_steps.say: The wavelength is 0.12 m, about 12 cm.

silver.display: A wave has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate its frequency, then find the wavelength if the wave speed is 5 m/s.
silver.equation_hint: Given on equation sheet: \(T = \frac{1}{f}\), then \(v = f\lambda\)
silver.hint: Find frequency (f = 1 ÷ T) first, then λ = v ÷ f.

misconceptions.message: f = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz, then λ = 5 ÷ 50 = 0.1 m. Stopping at 50 gives the frequency, not the wavelength.

guided_steps.say: Two steps. First frequency from the period: \(f = 1 \div T\).
Now the wavelength: \(\lambda = v \div f\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 5 m/s, so λ = 0.1 m.

gold.display: A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together and move off. Calculate the velocity after the collision.
gold.hint: Total momentum before = total momentum after; divide by the combined mass.

misconceptions.message: After they stick, combined mass = 3 + 1 = 4 kg. v = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m/s. Using only 3 kg gives 4.

guided_steps.say: Momentum is conserved: total \(mv\) before equals total after. Find the momentum before.
guided_steps.hint: Only the moving trolley has momentum.

guided_steps.pre: After they stick, the combined mass = 3 + 1 =

guided_steps.say: That 12 kg m/s is shared by 4 kg. \(v = p \div m\).

guided_steps.done: Matches the 12 kg m/s before, so v = 3 m/s.

gold.display: A 0.05 kg bullet is fired at 400 m/s into a 2.95 kg block of wood on a frictionless surface. The bullet embeds in the block. Calculate the velocity of the block and bullet after the collision.
gold.hint: Momentum before = bullet only; divide by the total mass after.

misconceptions.message: Total mass after = 0.05 + 2.95 = 3 kg. v = 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 m/s. Using only 2.95 kg gives 6.78.

guided_steps.say: Momentum is conserved. The bullet carries all the momentum before.

guided_steps.hint: Bullet plus block, now stuck together.

guided_steps.say: That 20 kg m/s is shared by 3 kg. \(v = p \div m\).

guided_steps.hint: Momentum divided by your velocity. Round to the nearest whole.
guided_steps.done: Back to 3 kg, so v = 6.67 m/s.

gold.display: A rocket of mass 500 kg fires its engines, producing a thrust of 8000 N. Its weight is 4900 N. Calculate the resultant force and the acceleration.
gold.hint: Resultant force = thrust − weight, then a = F ÷ m.

misconceptions.message: Resultant = thrust − weight = 8000 − 4900 = 3100 N. a = 3100 ÷ 500 = 6.2 m/s². Using 8000 N gives 16.

guided_steps.say: Find the resultant force: thrust up minus weight down.
guided_steps.hint: Weight pulls down, so subtract it.

guided_steps.say: Now \(a = F \div m\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 3100 N, so a = 6.2 m/s².

gold.display: A radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz. The speed of radio waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the wavelength in standard form.
gold.hint: Convert MHz to Hz (× 10⁶), then λ = v ÷ f; give the answer in standard form.

misconceptions.message: 98.5 MHz = 9.85 × 10⁷ Hz. λ = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ (9.85 × 10⁷) = 3.05 × 10⁰ m. Forgetting to convert MHz gives 3.05 × 10⁶.

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\), rearranged to \(\lambda = v \div f\). Give the answer in standard form. First fix the frequency.
guided_steps.pre: 98.5 MHz = 98.5 × 10⁶ Hz. Written as A × 10⁷, A =

guided_steps.say: Now the powers of ten.

guided_steps.hint: Move the decimal one place right. To 2 d.p.

guided_steps.pre: In standard form the number in front sits between 1 and 10. 3.05 already does, so λ = 3.05 × 10ⁿ, where n =
guided_steps.hint: 3.05 needs no further shift, so the power is zero.
guided_steps.done: The wavelength is 3.05 m, written 3.05 × 10⁰ m.

gold.display: A car of mass 1000 kg accelerates at 2 m/s² for 8 seconds. The driving force is 3200 N. Calculate the friction force acting on the car.
gold.hint: Resultant = m × a, then friction = driving − resultant.

misconceptions.message: Resultant = ma = 2000 N. Friction = driving − resultant = 3200 − 2000 = 1200 N. Adding gives 5200.

guided_steps.say: First the resultant force from \(F = ma\).
guided_steps.hint: Mass times acceleration. The 8 seconds is not needed.

guided_steps.say: Friction is what is left: driving force minus resultant.
guided_steps.hint: Take the resultant off the driving force.
It should equal the resultant force.
guided_steps.done: Gives back the resultant 2000 N, so friction = 1200 N.

gold.display: An X-ray has a wavelength of \(1 \times 10^{-10}\) m. The speed of EM waves is \(3 \times 10^8\) m/s. Calculate the frequency of the X-ray. Give your answer in standard form.
gold.hint: Rearrange v = fλ to f = v ÷ λ; subtract the powers of ten.

misconceptions.message: f = v ÷ λ. Dividing subtracts the powers: 8 − (−10) = 18, so f = 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz. Adding them by mistake gives 10⁻².

guided_steps.say: The equation is \(v = f\lambda\), rearranged to \(f = v \div \lambda\). Give the answer in standard form.
guided_steps.hint: Just the fronts of each number.

guided_steps.say: Now the powers of ten. Dividing subtracts them, and subtracting a negative adds.

guided_steps.pre: Check by reversing: v = f × λ, so the powers add: 18 + (−10) =
guided_steps.done: Gives 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the original speed, so f = 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz.

problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, values already in the right units: substitute straight in.
problem_bank.silver_description: Convert units first, or rearrange the equation, or find the resultant force before substituting.
problem_bank.gold_description: Two steps chained: momentum conservation, standard form, or a resultant force feeding into F = ma.

worked_examples.question: A resultant force of 600 N acts on a 50 kg object. Calculate its acceleration.
A car has a driving force of 4000 N and friction of 1200 N. Its mass is 1400 kg. Calculate its acceleration.
A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. They stick together. Calculate the velocity after the collision.

steps.label: Step 1: Momentum before
steps.content: p = mv. Trolley A: 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s. Trolley B: 1 × 0 = 0. Total = 6 kg m/s

steps.label: Step 2: Momentum after (conservation)
steps.content: Total mass = 2 + 1 = 3 kg. p = mv, so 6 = 3 × v

bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, units already right
steps: Choose the recall equation the question points to: \(F = ma\), \(v = f\lambda\) or \(T = 1/f\).
If you need something other than the subject, rearrange first: \(a = F/m\), \(f = v/\lambda\).
Substitute the numbers, calculate, and write the unit.

example.question: A resultant force of 30 N acts on a 6 kg mass. Calculate its acceleration.

silver.title: Silver: convert units or rearrange first
steps: Convert everything to base units before you substitute: grams to kilograms (÷ 1000), kHz to Hz (× 1000), cm to metres (÷ 100).
For a resultant force, subtract friction or weight from the driving force, then use \(a = F/m\).
Rearrange the equation for the quantity you want, then substitute and check.

example.question: A 200 g ball is pushed with 5 N against 1 N of friction. Calculate its acceleration.

gold.title: Gold: two steps chained
steps: Some problems need two equations. Momentum: total \(mv\) before a collision equals total \(mv\) after.
Find the intermediate value first (a resultant force, a combined mass, or a frequency), then feed it into the second equation.
For very large or very small numbers, give the answer in standard form.

example.question: A 2 kg trolley at 5 m/s hits a stationary 3 kg trolley and they stick together. Calculate their combined velocity.

opener.label: Before any equations
opener.display:
Same push. Empty trolley: it leaps.
Trolley loaded with shopping: it barely moves.

steps.say: Forget equations for a second. Picture two balls on a smooth floor.
steps.pre: A 2 kg ball needs a 10 N push to speed up at a certain rate. To make a 4 kg ball, twice as heavy, speed up at the SAME rate, how many newtons do you need?
steps.hint: Twice the mass needs twice the push.

steps.say: You just felt Newton's second law: force = mass × acceleration, \(F = ma\). Double the mass, double the force for the same acceleration.
steps.pre: Turn it around. For the 2 kg ball, that 10 N push gives an acceleration of 10 ÷ 2 =

steps.say: So \(a = F/m\). That one equation, plus \(p = mv\) for momentum and \(v = f\lambda\) for waves, is this whole lesson.

bronze.display: A resultant force of 60 N acts on a 15 kg box. Calculate its acceleration.
bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: The equation is \(F = ma\). We want the acceleration, so rearrange to \(a = F \div m\).

steps.done: Back to 60 N, so a = 4 m/s². Gone in one move.

silver.display: A 250 g ball is pushed with 3 N against 1 N of friction. Calculate its acceleration.
silver.label: Together: the silver move

steps.say: This one hides two traps: the mass is in grams, and there is friction. Convert the mass first.

steps.hint: Take the friction off the push.

steps.done: Back to 2 N, so a = 8 m/s². Convert and subtract: that was the whole point.

gold.display: A 2 kg trolley moving at 6 m/s hits a stationary 4 kg trolley. They stick together. Calculate the velocity after the collision.
gold.label: Together: the gold move

steps.say: Momentum is conserved: total \(mv\) before equals total after. Find it before the collision.
steps.hint: Only the moving trolley has momentum.

steps.say: That 12 kg m/s is now shared by 6 kg. \(v = p \div m\).

steps.done: Matches the 12 before, so v = 2 m/s. Conservation is the whole trick.
